title: Why Is the Area of a Circle Pi R Squared?
sources: Archimedes, 'Measurement of a Circle' (c. 260 BC), Proposition 1: the area of a circle equals a right triangle with one leg the radius and the other the circumference, i.e. (1/2) x 2 pi r x r = pi r^2. Harvard archive translation: https://legacy-www.math.harvard.edu/archive/archimedes09/pdf/Measurement.of.the.Circle.pdf

Wikipedia, 'Area of a circle' (rearrangement proof: sectors rearranged into a near-parallelogram that tends to a rectangle of width pi r and height r; the picture is credited to Nicholas of Cusa, Leonardo da Vinci and Sato Moshun, not Archimedes): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_of_a_disk

lines.text: Why is the area of a circle pi r squared?
lines.caps: Why is the *area | of a *circle | pi r *squared?

lines.text: Well, take a circle, and slice it like a pizza,
lines.caps: Take a *circle, | slice it like a *pizza

lines.text: Now flip every other wedge upside down, and line them up side by side.
lines.caps: Flip every *other one | line them *up | side by *side.

lines.text: It looks like a bumpy parallelogram.
Slice thinner and thinner, and the bumps flatten out,
Its height is just the radius, r.
And its width is half the crust, half the circumference,
lines.caps: Its *width is | half the *crust, | half the *circumference

lines.text: So the area is pi r times r.
lines.caps: So the *area | is pi r *times r.

lines.text: Archimedes proved this more than two thousand years ago,
with nothing but a circle and a clever cut.
